claims.text: A data-driven approach incorporating compositional-complexity and lattice-distortion descriptors can accurately identify single-phase high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
Alloys identified by the approach will have measured phonon thermal conductivity at least 15% lower than values predicted by conventional ab initio or semi-empirical methods.
Structural disorder increases phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
The target materials are near-equiatomic, single-phase solid solutions containing five or more elements.
The predictive model uses regression or machine-learning techniques trained on available high-entropy-alloy data.
The model can screen candidate compositions for low thermal conductivity before synthesis.
The range 300–800 K is relevant to thermal-insulation applications.
Compositional and structural disorder reduces phonon mean free paths within the alloy.
Local chemical complexity produces phonon scattering through lattice distortion, mass fluctuations, and strain fields.
The resulting phonon scattering reduces heat transport relative to simpler alloys.
The approach is primarily applicable to single-phase high-entropy alloys with moderate compositional spreads and validated training data.
The approach may be unreliable for multiphase or metastable systems outside its training range.
Experimental data are limited for some high-entropy-alloy compositions.
Model accuracy may vary in underrepresented compositional regions and at extreme temperatures.
Failure of measured thermal conductivity to fall at least 15% below the conventional prediction for the same composition would falsify the hypothesis.
